For a NAFDAC facility inspection, what you need depends on the scale of your factory. Let me walk you through the main requirements.

**Before the inspection itself**, your facility must meet NAFDAC's standards [1]. The exact requirements vary by scale:

- **Micro scale:** a purpose-built structure or dedicated part of a building with its own entrance and exit, insect-proof screens, good ventilation and lighting, food-grade equipment, a hand-washing station, proper waste disposal, and fumigation every three months. Your staff need basic education or training and proper protective gear (overalls, head covers, masks, gloves). You'll need to keep distribution records so you can recall products if needed [1].

- **Small scale:** the same as micro scale, plus at least two dedicated rooms separated from living areas, quality control testing of each batch by a public analyst, and documented investigation of any consumer complaints [1].

- **Standard (medium/large):** at least four rooms (cloak room, material store, production, finished product store), a fence at least five feet high, treated water (chlorinated, filtered and UV-sterilised), separate quality control staff with at least an OND qualification, and comprehensive stability studies [1].

**For the inspection application**, you'll need to submit these documents [1]:
- An application letter to NAFDAC's Director-General (Food Safety and Applied Nutrition Directorate)
- Your CAC business registration or business name certificate
- Trademark registration
- Coloured product label artwork (front, back, whole and side views)
- Company organogram with staff names, roles and qualifications
- Appointment letters and credentials for key personnel
- Standard operating procedures for production, quality control, cleaning, complaints and recalls
- Food handler medical certificates for your production staff
- List of raw materials and their sources
- Certificates of analysis for your finished product and raw materials
- List of production equipment
- Staff training and education certificates
- Certificate of fumigation

You'll apply through the NAFDAC product registration portal (NAPAMS). The guidelines list the address as www.napams.org, but **confirm the current portal address with NAFDAC** (0700-1-NAFDAC) before you start, as that address was not working recently [1].

The inspection fee depends on your scale: micro scale ₦11,000, small scale ₦30,000, or medium/large ₦40,000 [1]. However, the fee you'll actually pay is generated on the portal invoice, so **confirm the current fee with NAFDAC before paying** [1].

The PCN (Pharmacy Council of Nigeria) has strict rules about where a retail pharmacy can be located and how it must be built [1].

**Where you can site a pharmacy:**

You cannot open a pharmacy in a motor park, petrol station, market, clustered environment, kiosk, container or stall [1]. 

If you're opening a standalone pharmacy, it must be at least **200 metres** from another standalone pharmacy, and also at least 200 metres from any pharmacy in a shopping centre [1]. Distances are measured from front main door to front main door by the shortest accessible route [1].

If you're placing your pharmacy in a shopping centre, no more than three pharmacies are allowed in that centre, they cannot be next door to each other, and there must be at least five shops between them [1]. Patent medicine shops must be at least 400 metres away from your pharmacy [1].

The area around your pharmacy must stay sanitary. If the surroundings later become clustered or a market grows around it, you'll need to relocate within two years [1].

**The building itself:**

Your pharmacy needs a minimum floor area of **30 square metres**, with concrete walls, concrete or tiled floors, and a ceiling at least 3.05 metres high [1]. You'll need separate areas for dispensing, counselling, patient care, client waiting and storage, plus an office for the superintendent pharmacist [1]. The space must have good lighting and ventilation, with **functional air conditioning and fans** [1]. You'll also need fire extinguishers, a sand bucket and emergency exits [1].

These standards took effect in January 2025, so confirm the current requirements with your PCN state office before you start building [1].

To apply for the SON MANCAP certificate for locally made furniture, you'll need to follow a process that starts before the application itself [1].

**First, confirm your product and standard.** Contact your nearest SON state office to confirm that your furniture type needs MANCAP and to find out which Nigerian Industrial Standard applies to it [1]. You can also browse standards at https://son.gov.ng/standards/.

**Then apply for MANCAP.** You can apply in two ways [1]:
- Contact your nearest SON state office to get the application form, or
- Apply online at https://mancap.son.gov.ng/

**Documents you'll need to submit [1]:**
- Your CAC certificate of incorporation (so you'll need to register with CAC first if you haven't already)
- An on-the-spot test report of your furniture. If that test isn't comprehensive, you'll also need a laboratory report from SON or from a laboratory accredited by the Institute of Public Analysts of Nigeria (IPAN)
- Proof of payment for the application form and certification fees

**After approval, SON will inspect your factory.** You'll need at least two quarterly factory inspections, and your products must meet all the requirements of the relevant Nigerian Industrial Standard [1].

**Once everything passes, you'll get your certificate.** SON typically issues the MANCAP certificate within 60 days of receiving your complete application [1]. The certificate is valid for three years, and you'll get a numbered MANCAP logo that you can fix to each piece of furniture or print on labels. Your factory will be inspected every quarter while the certificate is valid [1].
